value.value: A Declare front end is one self-contained artifact — small enough to hold in your head, strict enough for a machine to verify, rich enough for an ambitious application. This is what Declare’s runtime does to make that true.

Declare asks you to believe something unusual about an application’s front end: that it’s complete. Everything the interface does is written in the one program — where each box goes, how a paragraph wraps, what a click landed on, how a view becomes the next one, how a list of a million rows scrolls on a phone. It can be written that way because the program states the relationships between its elements rather than the steps that maintain them — which is both easier to understand and substantially more compact. A machine can verify it whole. And because the compiler sees every relationship in advance, the runtime never has to discover anything while it runs — which is why it was possible to write its hot path once, in a few kilobytes of C.

A promise like that puts a demand on what runs underneath. If the browser decided the layout, the program wouldn’t be complete. If a click were routed by the DOM, the same interface drawn directly to pixels would route it differently. So the runtime makes those decisions itself, once — and then hands the browser everything it is genuinely best at: real text, native fields, the page’s own scroll, links that behave like links. Declare isn’t a native framework running in a browser tab; it’s a language for interfaces with the feel of good native software that are also good citizens of the web — crawlable, selectable, responsive, touch-native. That the same program also runs drawn directly to pixels, and in a Mac application with no browser in it, is the proof that it really is complete: nothing about it was ever decided somewhere else. Figure 1 is that division of labor, before and after.
Fig. 1 — Two pictures of one program

Left: the stack a web framework implies — your file, a framework, and a browser that decides layout, text, and what you touched. Right: what runs — the compiled program, the library (itself written in Declare), a runtime that owns every one of those decisions, a small C kernel beneath it, and a host on the far side of one interface that realizes the result. The same five colors mark the same layers throughout.

value.value: The compiler is where completeness is enforced. It parses the brackets into a tree, resolves every bare name to an explicit path, extracts the read set of every { } body, and type-checks each one as TypeScript against the real interface of every component — so an attribute that doesn’t exist, or a relationship that reads something it can’t, is an error before anything runs. What it emits is not code that builds a UI. It is a description of one: the tree with its attributes, a graph of which value reads which, and — for every body that is plain arithmetic over numeric slots — bytecode for a small stack machine.
One line from the homepage’s bouncing-ball demo, as it appears in the compiled artifact:

That last line never runs as JavaScript. In the calendar about 600 bodies take this path; the rest compile to ordinary functions the runtime calls back when their inputs change. A framework learns what depends on what while it runs — by re-running a component, or from a list you keep by hand. Here it is read off the source once, and the runtime never has to discover anything.

Because the program is data, it can be questioned as data. The Inspector on any page here — ⌥⌘D — reads this same graph: click a value and it shows the body that produced it, every path that body read, and their live values. That is not a debugging layer added to the runtime. It is the compiler’s output, still present at run time, answering a query.

When a handler writes an attribute, nothing updates yet. The write is queued. When the handler returns, the runtime performs one update: it finds every value that read what changed, recomputes each exactly once, in dependency order, and only then tells the host what moved. Declare calls that update a settle — the graph, disturbed by a write, coming back to rest — and it is the whole of the update model. If you know React, it is the nearest thing to a commit, except that nothing was rendered to compare against: the graph already knows what depends on what. The whole trip takes about a millisecond.
Fig. 2 — What a click sets in motion

The meter is live; its button is a library Button. Raise the level, then step through what your click set in motion. Four lanes: host, runtime, your code, kernel. Steps 5 and 6 are the split the compiler arranged in advance — arithmetic runs in the kernel; a template string is not arithmetic, so the kernel calls back into your compiled TypeScript, inside the same settle.

Steps 2 and 3 are the ones a web framework leaves to the browser: which element is under the pointer, and whether this was a click or the start of a drag. Here the runtime answers both, so hover, press, click-versus-drag and gesture ownership are one implementation — the same under a finger as under a pointer, and the same on every renderer.

Step 5 runs no JavaScript at all. Beneath the runtime sits a kernel: one C file, about 1,000 lines, that holds the graph’s tables — every attribute, every edge, the settle’s order — and evaluates the arithmetic the compiler turned into bytecode. In the browser it ships as WebAssembly, 11 KB gzipped inside the bundle; on the Mac the same source is linked in natively. It is unusual for a web framework to carry a C library, and it is only possible because the compiler left nothing for the runtime to work out: with every dependency and every arithmetic body known in advance, the bookkeeping of a settle is a fixed procedure over fixed tables, which is what C is for. A frame that only moves geometry — most animation frames — finishes inside it without entering JavaScript.

Continuity — a view becoming the next one rather than being replaced by it — is the part of good native software that is usually bespoke. Here is what makes it ordinary at run time. A Spring is an attribute with a target; each frame it writes its next value, and that write is a settle like any other — the same graph, the same kernel, the same dependency order. Nothing about animation is special-cased. Because geometry arithmetic runs as bytecode, a frame that only moves things — most frames of most animations — completes inside the kernel, in WebAssembly, and never enters JavaScript. Because a settle is one indivisible step, a new target arriving mid-flight is simply the next write: the spring retargets from wherever it is, and every value that read it follows. Interruptibility isn’t a feature of the animation system; it is what a reactive graph does when you write to it. And a layout is re-derived in the same settle, so an arrangement can travel as one thing — the calendar’s four views are one surface under a moving rectangle, and each frame of that zoom is a settle over the same few hundred kernel bodies.

Open a Declare page in the browser’s element inspector and every view is there — a div per component, nested to mirror the tree — with its position and size written on it as inline style and no layout CSS anywhere. That is not a shortcut. It is the division of labor: every box is decided before the host hears about it, by one of three things. Arithmetic over slots (x = { parent.width - 40 }) runs in the kernel. A layout is a library class with one method, place(), returning a box per child — 1.8 KB of runtime applies it. An unset width is the bounding box of the visible children, kept current as a rule over the geometry table. Text is the one place the host contributes a number: it measures glyph widths. Wrapping, line count and the resulting height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer.

Because the runtime placed every box, it can answer the inverse question — what is under this point? — and that answer decides hover, press, whether a gesture was a click, and where a drag lands. The scene below computes none of it. Each view is reporting its own hovered fact, kept true by the same walk that routes a press.
Fig. 3 — Ask the runtime what is under the pointer

Try the rotated card’s corners, the empty-looking glass, the badge, and the child where the pane’s clip cuts it off. The walk runs in reverse paint order and stops at the first view that has declared an interest in the pointer.

Drawn to pixels, or on the Mac, there is no DOM to ask, so this walk is the whole of hit-testing: clips subtracted, transforms inverted, scrollers corrected. In the DOM the browser names the element and the runtime resolves it to the nearest view with a handler. Either way the decision is one implementation, and the same one that decides whether a touch is a tap, a scroll, or a drag the page should not claim. Your program can ask it directly — app.viewAt(x, y) — which is how drag and drop is written.

Everything above happens on one side of a single interface. It is called Surface, it has 60 methods — setX, setFill, setText, setDrawing — the runtime calls them and a backend implements them, and a view never learns which backend it has. Below that interface a backend does one job: realize what it was told. The DOM backend keeps a div per view with its geometry as inline style, and hands the platform what the platform does best — real text that selects and finds, the page’s own scroll, links that ⌘-click, native form fields. The canvas backend draws the whole tree directly to pixels, with its own compositor and its own scroll physics, for surfaces that must be uniform or capturable. The Mac host is a Swift application with no web engine in it: it runs the same runtime bundle in JavaScriptCore, links the same kernel as C, and applies one batch of drawing operations per settle to a tree of Core Animation layers.

The calendar’s build, drawn to scale by gzipped bytes. Switch hosts and watch what moves: the program, the library and the rest of the runtime are the same bytes; one block is exchanged, and on the Mac the kernel leaves the bundle for the executable. Beneath, the same desktop program with the same four windows open, on each host.

Drawing crosses the interface the same way. A view that needs a mark attributes can’t express — a gauge, a sparkline, an icon — defines draw(d). It looks like canvas code but it records; the recording is plain data that the DOM backend rasterizes into the view’s own element, the canvas backend replays during its composite, and the Mac replays through Core Graphics. A drawing that read nothing that changed costs nothing.

Declare’s own model is single-threaded by construction: a settle is one step, and there is nothing in the language that runs concurrently with it. That is what lets hosts thread freely on their side of Surface — the canvas backend rasterizes drawings in a worker, and the Mac runs the runtime on a thread of its own and commits to the display on another. Your program never sees any of it.

Surface is the boundary between the runtime and its host. There is a second boundary, between a Declare program and code that isn’t Declare, and it has the same shape in every direction. A page embeds a Declare app by marking a sized element as its host — one attribute, data-declare-embed — and the app runs in that box like any other element on the page. The interface between them is declared, not improvised: the page provides values the app reads with hostProvided, the app exposes values the page reads back, and either side can post a message the other receives in onPost. Inside a Declare program the same contract runs the other way. A DOMIsland is a box the tree sizes and positions, inside which a video player, an editor or a React widget owns its own DOM. An AppIsland hosts a second Declare program as a tenant with the same provides, exposes and post — this article is one, mounted inside the homepage, taking its theme and type from the page around it. Three directions, one boundary, one vocabulary.

A Declare app in a browser is a web page, not an imitation of one. The behaviors that make a page a page stay the browser’s, and Declare does not simulate them: text is real text — it selects, it finds, it copies; fields are native fields, with native carets and input methods; scroll and overscroll are the page’s own; links are links, ⌘-click and all, and the Back button tells the truth; a crawler reads a static extraction from a plain host. The DOM renderer is the default because nothing about the program’s meaning is at stake in the browser, so all of that can be left to the browser without risk. A reader would struggle to tell a Declare page from any other.

What keeps that description honest is the second rendering. A program that owns its own semantics — no stylesheet, no browser layout engine to defer to — can be checked against another realization of itself, and the platform’s test suite holds the DOM renderer and the pixel renderer to the same picture on every change. The discipline that makes a front end complete is the same one that makes it mean exactly one thing.
